September 29th, all snow hell breaks loose

I'm up in the interior of Alaska and winter just landed with a bang. On the 25th we received a record snowfall. This was a heavy wet snow in an area not acustomed to heavy snow. This caused trees to bend down onto the lines and begin to open circuits up. I thought I would share some insights on these sort of situations from the ground level. I'm typing this on my cell so there will be spelling mistakes and such.

The situation at this time: -Power was knocked out to around 20k people in the area surrounding the town of Fairbanks. The 2nd largest city in our great state.

-Outside temps are around feeezing. This means the snow is very wet. Snow up here is usually very dry and easy to handle, this stuff is not.

-Each feeder line is plagued by trees being bent over by the snow load and taking down lines with it.

I suggest reading through the events logged on the GVEA (our electric coop) page. The storm was expected but the level of need wasn't.

When people began to lose power, the stores had a run on AAA batteries and bottled water. I suspect most people have headlamps up here and the most common cell i've seem for them is the AAA. Water is the stuff of life and even though we've got tons of snow around, it melts down to very little and it is very dirty. My home has a water tank but to access it I would have to take my pump loose. For a "short term" outage of 3 days, we've decided to run with snow melt for toilet flushes and bottled and jugged water for everything else.

Home depot and rental agencies ran out of generators for sale or rent quickly. I saw a dust covered display model going out the door the afternoon of the storm. Moreover, nobody had seemed to test their setups. One guy was looking for the parts to adapt a 15 amp plug to a 25 amp socket. Electricians on voat will cringe at that idea but people will do all kinds of things to keep their house warm.

Part 2:

The first major infrastructure failure I saw was the trouble desk number for our electric co. When the snow hit the trees, calling the trouble desk wouldn't even get a ring. In the end, facebook had an email address posted to report outages with. It seems silly but a person working in the dispatch center can fire off a quick reply faster than dictating things over the phone.

The next failure has been the cell phone towers. They do have backups but one of our major providers has reported they will start seeing their towers drop soon. Landlines are also carried on the same poles as the power lines so, in this case, they have failed frequently as well. In our family we have phones on various providers so we've been able to relay messages around.

If you look at the top of the GVEA page, you'll see a reference to "if there is an emergency, diall 911 and they will send someone out or give you the location of your nearest fire station". Think about that one for a bit. The 911 service will run around full capacity on normal days. On bad days all hands will be on deck but that will not mean a 1000% increase in capacity. We're only a few days into this thing and already we're seeing a reduction in service and triage.
